splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any one criterion disqualifies).
splits.description: The circuits are deeply split on whether a defendant must meet all three criminal-history disqualifiers listed in § 3553(f)(1) to be excluded from safety-valve relief, or whether meeting any single criterion is disqualifying. This affects whether district courts must sentence below statutory minimums for drug offenses, with identical defendants receiving vastly different sentences depending on the circuit.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1).

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria disqualifies the defendant from safety-valve relief.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity takes priority over agency/Sentencing Commission deference (Auer/Kisor deference) when interpreting ambiguous criminal sentencing provisions.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether lenity should trump deference to agency interpretations in criminal contexts. At least three circuits hold lenity prevails, while the Third Circuit has held that agency deference trumps lenity. The issue has become more significant after Loper Bright overruled Chevron deference.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes priority over agency or Sentencing Commission deference when interpreting ambiguous criminal provisions, preventing agencies from expanding criminal liability through interpretive guidance.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency or Sentencing Commission deference takes priority over the rule of lenity, allowing anti-defendant readings of ambiguous provisions when supported by authoritative agency interpretation.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines' commentary (Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2) can authoritatively expand the definition of 'controlled substance offense' to include inchoate offenses like conspiracy, when the guideline text does not mention them.
splits.description: Circuits have divided on whether Application Note 1's inclusion of conspiracy and other inchoate offenses as 'controlled substance offenses' is a valid, authoritative interpretation of § 4B1.2, or whether the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses and the commentary impermissibly expands its scope. The Sentencing Commission has since amended the guideline text, but the split affects many pending cases.

positions.label: Commentary validly includes inchoate offenses
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is an authoritative interpretation of § 4B1.2(b) under Stinson, and that conspiracy and other inchoate offenses qualify as controlled substance offenses for career-offender purposes.

positions.label: Commentary cannot expand beyond guideline text
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text of § 4B1.2(b) unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses, and Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the definition beyond what the text supports, especially after Kisor narrowed deference to agency interpretations.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a prior state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state schedule covers substances not listed on the federal Controlled Substances Act schedules.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires the substance underlying a state conviction to also be federally controlled. Some circuits hold state convictions qualify regardless of federal scheduling, while others require a match to federal schedules. This affects career-offender designations and base offense levels for many defendants.

positions.label: State law controls — no federal match required
positions.summary: Holds that an 'offense under state law' qualifies as a controlled substance offense under the Guidelines even if the particular substance is not controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

positions.label: Federal match required
positions.summary: Holds that a prior state drug conviction qualifies as a controlled substance offense under the Guidelines only if the substance at issue is also controlled under federal law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A), and whether the Sentencing Commission's policy statement (U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6)) permitting this exceeds its statutory authority.
splits.description: Circuits have divided on whether non-retroactive sentencing changes can support compassionate release motions. The Seventh and Eighth Circuits hold that such changes cannot contribute to extraordinary and compelling reasons, while other circuits have permitted them. The Sentencing Commission's 2024 amendment to § 1B1.13(b)(6) attempted to resolve this but has itself been challenged as exceeding the Commission's authority.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, whether alone or combined with other factors, cannot constitute an extraordinary and compelling reason for a sentence reduction under § 3582(c)(1)(A), and the Sentencing Commission lacks authority to override this through a policy statement.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes can support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in sentencing law may be considered, alone or in combination with other factors, as extraordinary and compelling reasons warranting compassionate release under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may impose sentences upon revocation of supervised release to punish the defendant for the violation, or whether revocation sentences must be limited to purposes related to the original offense and reentry into society.
splits.description: The Sixth Circuit permits district courts to expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release conditions, while other circuits hold that revocation sentences must relate to the breach of trust from the original offense and cannot serve as standalone punishment for the new violation. This affects hundreds of revocation proceedings annually.

positions.label: Punishment for violation is permissible
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may impose revocation sentences that expressly punish defendants for their violations of supervised release conditions.

positions.label: Punishment for violation is not permissible
positions.summary: Holds that revocation sentences must be based on the breach of trust from the original offense and the need for reentry supervision, not as punishment for the supervised release violation itself.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners challenging the conditions or execution of their confinement (as opposed to the fact or duration of imprisonment) must proceed via habeas corpus or may bring civil rights actions, and whether habeas corpus is available for such claims.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether habeas corpus is the exclusive remedy for challenges to conditions or execution of confinement, or whether prisoners may also use civil rights statutes like Bivens or § 1983. This split affects federal prisoners challenging BOP decisions on matters like First Step Act time credits, prerelease custody, and other aspects of sentence execution.

positions.label: Habeas available for conditions/execution challenges
positions.summary: Holds that habeas corpus under 28 U.S.C. § 2241 is available to challenge conditions or execution of confinement, including BOP decisions regarding statutory rights under the First Step Act.

positions.label: Civil rights actions are the proper vehicle
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to conditions of confinement or execution-related BOP decisions should be brought through civil rights actions rather than habeas, because they do not challenge the fact or duration of imprisonment.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the appeal deadline for a Hyde Amendment attorney's fees order is governed by the civil notice-of-appeal deadline (30 days) or the criminal deadline (14 days).
splits.description: Circuits have split on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees in a criminal case is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case (triggering the 30-day civil appeal deadline) or is part of the criminal case itself (triggering the 14-day criminal deadline). The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies (30 days)
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 30-day civil appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a) applies.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies (14 days)
positions.summary: Holds that the Hyde Amendment motion is part of the criminal case, making the 14-day criminal appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b) applicable.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in equity of an asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to debtors who convert in good faith from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in property value between a Chapter 13 filing and a good-faith conversion to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtor. The Ninth Circuit held that such appreciation belongs to the estate, while other circuits have reached the opposite conclusion. This affects debtors' ability to retain equity growth during reorganization attempts.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that under the plain language of § 348(f)(1)(A) and § 541(a), post-petition appreciation in property value belongs to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that § 348(f)(1)(A) was designed to protect good-faith converting debtors, and post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation in property value belongs to the debtors, not the estate.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagreed on whether ERISA and MPPAA require actuarial assumptions used to calculate withdrawal liability to be set before the statutory measurement date or whether actuaries may select assumptions after that date. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers in multiemployer pension plans.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability must be determined by the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), providing employers with greater predictability.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that the actuary may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, as long as the assumptions are applied to data measured as of that date.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: New York Times Co. v. Newspaper & Mail Deliverers'-Publishers' Pension Fund

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts can apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the period of court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects how federal courts calculate sentencing guidelines at revocation hearings for thousands of individuals who abscond each year.

positions.label: Supervised release is tolled during absconding
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled when a supervisee absconds, so the clock does not run during the period of flight, extending the court's jurisdiction to revoke.

positions.label: Supervised release is not tolled
positions.summary: Holds that without explicit statutory authorization, courts cannot apply a judicially-created tolling doctrine to extend supervised release beyond the period specified in the judgment.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under 28 U.S.C. § 2255.
splits.description: The circuits have split 6-to-3 on whether federal prisoners face the categorical bar of § 2244(b)(1) — which prevents relitigating any claim previously presented — in addition to § 2255(h)'s own gatekeeping requirements. If (b)(1) applies, federal prisoners are subject to a stricter standard than Congress may have intended for successive collateral attacks.

positions.label: § 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously presented claims applies to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, imposing a categorical bar in addition to § 2255(h)'s requirements.

positions.label: § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s bar does not apply to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, meaning federal prisoners need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits have disagreed on the standards for evaluating whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures. The resolution of this question determines whether election-rule disputes are heard before or after elections, with significant implications for mail-in voting rules, ballot counting deadlines, and election administration nationwide.

positions.label: Candidate has standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates for federal office suffer a cognizable competitive injury sufficient for Article III standing when challenging state laws that alter voting procedures, even before any concrete vote dilution has occurred.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

positions.label: Candidate lacks standing
positions.summary: Holds that a candidate's generalized competitive interest is insufficient for Article III standing to challenge election administration rules without showing a more particularized injury.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The Supreme Court granted certiorari to review the Second Circuit's approach to legal questions regarding fair treatment standards, discrimination liability, and damages in the hospitality and service industries. The grant suggests a circuit split on the applicable legal framework for such claims.

positions.label: Second Circuit approach
positions.summary: Applied standards for discrimination claims in hospitality establishments that the Supreme Court found sufficiently important or unsettled to warrant review, suggesting a distinctive approach to liability and remedies.

positions.label: Other circuits' approach
positions.summary: Other circuits have applied different standards for evaluating discrimination claims in business establishments, creating the disagreement that prompted Supreme Court review.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
